UNIVERSIDAD POLITÉCNICA DE MADRID
Managing with Artificial Intelligence - T01
TASK 1
Inventory & Initial Scan
Purpose
Inventory the supplied Document Set, scan the papers for metadata and relevant fragments, and define the knowledge domain before deeper synthesis.
Document inventory and initial scan
Knowledge-domain boundary
The corpus defines a management problem at the intersection of steel-production scheduling, energy efficiency, uncertainty/resilience, Digital Twins, reinforcement learning, explainability and human/safety governance. The operational core is furnace/rolling/ladle/heat-treatment scheduling; energy and tardiness form recurring multi-objective criteria; uncertainty makes rescheduling necessary; Digital Twins and DRL provide adaptive capabilities; XAI and human oversight address trust and deployment risk.
Initial scan findings
Scheduling and energy are the densest themes: many papers optimize furnace, rolling, ladle or heat-treatment decisions while reducing energy consumption or cost.
Uncertainty is structural rather than exceptional: machine breakdowns, variable release/processing times, market prices and changing plant states appear repeatedly.
Digital Twins act as a bridge between physical steel processes and adaptive AI by providing a synchronized/simulated environment.
DRL is positioned as an adaptive sequential decision mechanism, especially where the state changes faster than full rescheduling can be recomputed.
XAI, counterfactual explanations, process safety and human-centric planning are less numerous but strategically important because they address operator trust, challengeability and accountability.

UNIVERSIDAD POLITÉCNICA DE MADRID
Managing with Artificial Intelligence - T01
TASK 2
Topographical Mapping
Purpose
Map the knowledge extracted in Task 1 in two complementary ways: a hierarchical topic tree and a cross-reference network. The first shows structure; the second shows relationships across themes.
A. Hierarchical Topic Tree
Figure 1. Hierarchical Topic Tree derived from the 31 supplied papers.
The hierarchy places steel scheduling at the operational core, then separates energy/sustainability, uncertainty/resilience, digital intelligence, and trust/governance. Subtopics preserve the main process contexts found in the papers: furnaces, rolling, ladles, heat treatment, demand response, robust/online scheduling, Digital Twins, DRL and explainability.
B. Cross-Reference Network
Figure 2. Cross-reference network showing the strongest conceptual links.
Interpretation of the map
Scheduling ↔ Energy: production timing changes idle energy, furnace energy, electricity cost and demand-response value.
Scheduling ↔ Uncertainty: disruptions and variable processing/release times require proactive, robust or dynamic rescheduling.
Digital Twin ↔ DRL: the twin provides state representation, simulation and a safer environment for training/testing adaptive policies.
DRL ↔ Energy: learning-based policies can react to electricity prices, energy states and production conditions.
DRL ↔ XAI/Human: adaptive policies need understandable reasons, alternatives, monitoring and override mechanisms in high-stakes production.
Knowledge concentration is strongest around scheduling-energy optimization. XAI/human-centric work is more isolated, but it closes a deployment gap left by purely technical optimization papers.

UNIVERSIDAD POLITÉCNICA DE MADRID
Managing with Artificial Intelligence - T01
TASK 3
Synthesis Divergence
Purpose
Develop the key subtopics from the map, deliberately contrasting approaches and exposing trade-offs rather than forcing premature agreement.
Figure 1. Divergence map: competing objectives and design tensions.
Divergent synthesis by subtopic
Key trade-offs
Adaptability vs. guaranteed feasibility
DRL can adapt to changing states, but metallurgical, capacity and safety constraints should remain explicit. A hybrid architecture is safer than reward shaping alone.
Energy vs. service performance
Reducing energy or shifting loads can conflict with throughput, due dates, thermal constraints and schedule stability. The objective must therefore be multi-criteria.
Automation vs. human authority
The corpus supports intelligence augmentation as a practical first deployment: AI recommends; operators approve exceptional/high-impact actions.
Model sophistication vs. interpretability
Higher-performing black-box models can create adoption and audit problems. XAI helps, but must be combined with constraints, monitoring and rollback.
Simulation freedom vs. reality gap
A Digital Twin allows aggressive experimentation, but policies can exploit model errors. Calibration and out-of-distribution testing are essential.
Divergence conclusion
The synthesis rules out two extremes: a purely static/manual approach is insufficiently adaptive, while unconstrained autonomous DRL is too risky for first deployment. The viable design space is hybrid: explicit constraints + Digital Twin + adaptive AI + XAI + human governance.
Approach | What it contributes | Tension / limitation | Management role
Static mathematical / OR scheduling | Explicit objectives and hard constraints; auditable feasibility. | Can be slow or brittle when plant conditions change rapidly. | Use as baseline planner and hard-constraint layer.
Robust / proactive scheduling | Anticipates breakdowns and uncertainty. | Can become conservative; quality depends on uncertainty assumptions. | Use for critical disruption-prone stages.
Digital Twin | Safe what-if analysis, synchronization and policy validation. | Requires fidelity, data integration and continuous calibration. | Use as the experimentation and validation backbone.
Deep Reinforcement Learning | Adaptive sequential decisions and fast inference after training. | Training burden, reward design, generalization and safety risks. | Use for dynamic decisions inside a constrained action space.
XAI / counterfactual explanations | Makes recommendations understandable and challengeable. | An explanation is not a proof of correctness or safety. | Use for operator-facing justification, audit and learning.
Human-in-the-loop | Adds tacit knowledge, accountability and exception handling. | May slow decisions and introduce inconsistency. | Retain for high-impact or unfamiliar operating conditions.

UNIVERSIDAD POLITÉCNICA DE MADRID
Managing with Artificial Intelligence - T01
TASK 4
Integrative Synthesis
Purpose
Integrate the converging evidence from Tasks 1-3 into one organizational blueprint that connects steel-process constraints, Digital Twins, DRL, explainability and human decision rights.
Figure 1. Integrated organizational blueprint.
Blueprint components
1. Operational data layer
Connect MES/ERP, furnace/rolling/ladle states, IoT sensors, energy meters, maintenance events, order priorities and energy-market signals. Establish timestamp alignment, ownership and data-quality controls.
2. Digital Twin layer
Represent the current plant state and key process constraints. Use the twin for what-if scenarios, disruption simulation, model training and pre-deployment validation.
3. Hybrid decision engine
Use optimization/OR for baseline schedules and explicit feasibility. Use DRL for dynamic rescheduling or energy-aware decisions, but restrict actions to the feasible envelope.
4. XAI and safety gate
For each recommendation expose the main drivers, expected KPI effect, active constraints, a counterfactual alternative, and a confidence/novelty indicator.
5. Human execution and feedback
During the pilot, operators approve high-impact actions and record reasons for overrides. Repeatedly validated low-risk actions can later move to supervised automation.
Organizational roles and governance
Implementation sequence
Phase 0 - Baseline: freeze current KPIs, constraints and exception rules.
Phase 1 - Digital Twin: build and calibrate a minimum viable twin for one furnace/line.
Phase 2 - Shadow mode: run AI recommendations without controlling equipment; compare with current dispatching.
Phase 3 - Human-approved pilot: show explanations and require operator approval for actions.
Phase 4 - Bounded automation: automate only low-risk action classes after predefined safety, robustness and KPI gates are met.
Success metrics
Operational: throughput, tardiness, schedule stability, utilization and waiting time. Energy: energy per tonne, idle energy, peak demand and energy cost per tonne. Safety/quality: constraint violations and interventions. AI/governance: latency, out-of-distribution rate, acceptance/override rate and explanation usefulness.
Role | Responsibility
Operations | Own production objectives, dispatching workflow and operating procedures.
Process / metallurgical engineering | Own hard process, quality and metallurgical constraints.
Energy management | Own tariff assumptions, energy KPIs and demand-response rules.
Data / AI team | Own model development, monitoring, retraining and documentation.
IT / OT | Own integration, cybersecurity, availability and interfaces.
Safety / Quality | Approve deployment gates, exception handling and rollback procedures.

UNIVERSIDAD POLITÉCNICA DE MADRID
Managing with Artificial Intelligence - T01
TASK 5
Final Report & Strategic Storytelling
Executive Briefing using AIDA
A - Attention
Steel production scheduling is simultaneously an operations, energy and resilience problem. The supplied papers repeatedly connect furnace/rolling/ladle decisions with energy consumption or cost, while uncertainty from breakdowns, processing times and changing plant states reduces the usefulness of static schedules.
I - Interest
The corpus provides complementary tools. Robust and online scheduling manage disruption; Digital Twins create a synchronized and simulated environment; DRL can learn adaptive sequential decisions; XAI and counterfactuals can make those decisions understandable to operators. These technologies solve different layers of the same management problem.
D - Desire
A practical target is not a black-box autonomous scheduler. It is a constrained decision-intelligence system: engineering rules protect feasibility, the Digital Twin supports testing, DRL adapts within the feasible action space, XAI explains recommendations, and humans retain authority over high-impact or unfamiliar situations.
A - Action
Launch a bounded pilot on one furnace or production segment. Establish baseline KPIs and hard constraints; build/calibrate the minimum viable Digital Twin; benchmark current scheduling against a constrained DRL/optimization approach; add operator-facing explanations; run shadow mode; then human-approved mode; automate only after predefined safety, robustness, energy and service gates are satisfied.
Figure 1. Recommended target operating model.
Strategic recommendation
Adopt a Digital-Twin-first, constrained-DRL, explainable and human-governed pathway. The strategic value comes from the closed loop between reliable plant data, simulation, adaptive decision logic, explicit engineering constraints, explanations and operational feedback - not from DRL in isolation.
Decision gates before automation
No hard-constraint violations in validation scenarios.
Performance remains acceptable under simulated breakdowns and uncertainty.
Latency fits the operational decision window.
Unfamiliar/out-of-distribution states are detected and escalated.
Operators can understand, challenge and override recommendations.
Rollback and incident procedures are tested before live automation.
Conclusion
The five-task synthesis moves from evidence inventory, to knowledge mapping, to deliberate divergence, to integration, and finally to an executive action story. The recommended path progresses from visibility → simulation → recommendation → supervised automation, preserving safety and human accountability while pursuing energy and scheduling improvements.
